Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(0,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}- v^{2} + \cos{\left(u \right)}\\u + v\end{bmatrix}?
$$

Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))\approx\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\cdot\underbrace{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{\delta A}
$$

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}&\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix}\\& =\begin{vmatrix}- \sin{\left(u \right)}&- 2 v\\1&1\end{vmatrix}\\& =(- \sin{\left(u \right)})\cdot (1)-(- 2 v)\cdot (1)\\& =-\sin u+2v\\\left.\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|_{(0,2)} & =\left(2 v - \sin{\left(u \right)}\right)\big|_{u=0,v=2}\\& =2 (2) - \sin{\left((0) \right)}\\& =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & \approx|4|\cdot\delta A\\ & =4\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\left(u - 4\right)^{2} \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=\left(u - 4\right)^{2},\,y(u,v,w)=v,\,z(u,v,w)=w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2 u - 8 & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2 u - 8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(2 u - 8)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(2 u - 8)(1\cdot(1)-(0)\cdot(0)) \\  & =2 \left(u - 4\right).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 2 \left(u - 4\right) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The critical points lie on the plane $u - 4=0.$
The critical points lie on the plane $v - 4=0.$
The critical points lie on the plane $u + 4=0.$
The critical points lie on the plane $u=0.$
The critical points lie on the plane $u - 4=0.$
The critical points lie on the plane $w - 4=0.$

$$

$$

where $D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 4,\quad 0\le x + y\le 2\}.$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le x\le 4,\quad 0\le x + y\le 2,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x + y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):0\le u\le 4,\,0\le v\le 2\}.
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left|\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\right|\\&=1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=1=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\ne0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

Solving the transformation equations gives $x=u,\ y=- u + v$, so the transformation is one-to-one on this domain.

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$

$$

where $D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 5,\quad 0\le x^{2} + y\le 3\}.$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le x\le 5,\quad 0\le x^{2} + y\le 3,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x^{2} + y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):0\le u\le 5,\,0\le v\le 3\}.
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\end{vmatrix}\\&=\left|\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\2 x & 1\end{bmatrix}\right|\\&=1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\left(\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right)^{-1}=1=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\ne0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

Solving the transformation equations gives $x=u,\ y=- u^{2} + v$, so the transformation is one-to-one on this domain.

$$

Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=\left(- y\right)\,i+\left(x\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\left(3 \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(4 \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,j+\left(1 - t^{2}\right)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ=\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3 \cos{\left(\pi t \right)},\quad y=4 \sin{\left(\pi t \right)},\quad z=1 - t^{2}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\left(- y\right)\,i+\left(x\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k \\ & =\left(- 4 \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(3 \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(3 \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,i+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(4 \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,j+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(1 - t^{2}\right)\,k \\ & =\left(- 3 \pi \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(4 \pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,j+\left(- 2 t\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(\left(- 4 \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(3 \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k\right)\cdot\left(\left(- 3 \pi \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,i+\left(4 \pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,j+\left(- 2 t\right)\,k\right) \\ & =\left(- 4 \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\cdot\left(- 3 \pi \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)+\left(3 \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\cdot\left(4 \pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot\left(- 2 t\right) \\ & =\left(12 \pi \sin^{2}{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)+\left(12 \pi \cos^{2}{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =12 \pi\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ=\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr & =\int_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\int_{-1}^{1}\left(12 \pi\right)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\left[12 \pi t\right]_{-1}^{1} \\ & =[\left(12 \pi\right)]-[\left(- 12 \pi\right)] \\ & =24 \pi\end{aligned}

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F=-x\,\mathbf i+3y\,\mathbf j$ and a square $C$ with side length $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*

If $\mathbf F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds,
$$

where $\mathbf n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds+\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds\\
&\quad+\int_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_3\,\mathrm ds+\int_{C_4}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_4\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179647/images/flux-1.0.2-8c7428d2b40a578c2791-normals.png)

We compute this integral in two stages.

- First, consider the side $C_1.$ We have that $\mathbf n_1=\mathbf i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_1}(-x\,\mathbf i+3y\,\mathbf j)\cdot\mathbf i\,\mathrm ds\\
&=-\int_{C_1}x\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t)=1\mathbf i+t\,\mathbf j,\quad \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf j,\quad t\in[-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\int_{C_1}x\,\mathrm ds
&=-\int_{-1}^{1}1\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt\\
&=(-1)\int_{-1}^{1}\mathrm dt\\
&=(-1)\cdot 2\\
&=-2.
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_3$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds=\int_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_3\,\mathrm ds=-2.
$$

- Next, consider the side $C_2.$ We have that $\mathbf n_2=\mathbf j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_2}(-x\,\mathbf i+3y\,\mathbf j)\cdot\mathbf j\,\mathrm ds\\
&=3\int_{C_2}y\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_2,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+1\mathbf j,\quad \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf i,\quad t\in[-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
3\int_{C_2}y\,\mathrm ds
&=3\int_{-1}^{1}1\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt\\
&=(3)\int_{-1}^{1}\mathrm dt\\
&=(3)\cdot 2\\
&=6.
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_4$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds=\int_{C_4}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_4\,\mathrm ds=6.
$$

Finally, then

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds=2\cdot(-2)+2\cdot(6)=8.
$$

$$

Using the change of variables 

$$

$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(x - 4 y)^{2}-(y)=0$ and the line $y=9.$

The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x - 4 y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Substituting $x - 4 y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
(x - 4 y)^{2}-(y)=0\,⟹\,u^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v=u^{2}.
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
v=9.
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &=u^{2} \\ v &=9\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,u=\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 3,9).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-3\le u\le 3,\,u^{2}\le v\le 9\}.
$$

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186129197/plots/3a931359251be4c6f04a7150.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1&-4\\0&1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D dxdy &=\iint_Δ |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,dudv \\ &=\iint_Δ |1|\,dudv \\ &=1\int_{-3}^{3}[\int_{u^{2}}^{9}dv]du \\ &=1\int_{-3}^{3}[v]_{u^{2}}^{9}du \\ &=1\int_{-3}^{3}(9)-(u^{2})du \\ &=1\int_{-3}^{3}(9 - u^{2})du \\ &=1[- \frac{u^{3}}{3} + 9 u]_{-3}^{3} \\ &=1(((27)+(-9))-((-27)+(9))) \\ &=1(36) \\ &=36\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}

\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(2 x^{2} y\right)&=4 x y\\
f_x(x,y)&=\left(\frac{e^{u}}{e^{u} + 1}\right)\cdot\left(- 4 x\right)+\left(4 x y\right)\\
&=4 x y - \frac{4 x e^{- 2 x^{2} + y}}{e^{- 2 x^{2} + y} + 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=-1$ and $y=-2$ after differentiating. The inner input is

$$
u_0=- 2 \left(-1\right)^{2} + \left(-2\right)=-4.
$$

Using this value in the chain factors gives

&=\frac{4 \left(3 + 2 e^{4}\right)}{1 + e^{4}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

Which of the following statements are true regarding the matrix $B$?

Select all that apply.

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

A square matrix is singular if and only if its determinant is zero.

Expand along the top row, with signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\det(B) &= 0\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 8 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +(-4)\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\
&= 0\left(8-(-8)\right) \\
&\quad +(-4)\left(4-(0)\right) \\
&\quad +2\left(8-(0)\right) \\
&= 0\cdot 16 \\
&\quad +(-4)\cdot 4 \\
&\quad +2\cdot 8 \\
&= 0-16+16 \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(B)=0$, $B$ is singular.

Do not select “$\det(B)=16$.”

Do not select “$\det(B)=-32$.”

Select “$B$ is a singular matrix.”

The matrices $F$ and $A$ differ in just one entry. Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

$$
F=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

A square matrix is singular if and only if its determinant is zero. A singular matrix has no multiplicative inverse; a nonsingular square matrix has one. Compare both determinants rather than assuming that one changed entry changes singularity.

Expand along the top row, with signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\det(F) &= 1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +(-2)\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +(-1)\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\
&= 1\left(1-(-2)\right) \\
&\quad +(-2)\left(1-(-1)\right) \\
&\quad +(-1)\left(-2-(-1)\right) \\
&= 1\cdot 3 \\
&\quad +(-2)\cdot 2 \\
&\quad +(-1)\cdot (-1) \\
&= 3-4+1 \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\det(A) &= 1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +(-2)\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\
&\quad +(-1)\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\
&= 1\left(1-(0)\right) \\
&\quad +(-2)\left(1-(-1)\right) \\
&\quad +(-1)\left(0-(-1)\right) \\
&= 1\cdot 1 \\
&\quad +(-2)\cdot 2 \\
&\quad +(-1)\cdot 1 \\
&= 1-4-1 \\
&= -4
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(F)=0$, $F$ is singular.

Since $\det(A)=-4\ne0$, $A$ is **not** singular.

Consider the plane curve $2 x^{2} + 3 y^{2}=5.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at $(1,-1).$

Use $f(x,y)=2 x^{2} + 3 y^{2}.$ The nonzero gradient gives the direction of the normal line. A line through $(x_0,y_0)$ parallel to $\left\langle a,b\right\rangle$ satisfies $b(x-x_0)=a(y-y_0).$

Set

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)&=2 x^{2} + 3 y^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the curve gives the level set $f(x,y)=5.$ Compute the partial derivatives, holding the other coordinate fixed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=4 x \\
f_y(x,y)&=6 y \\
\nabla f(1,-1)&=\left\langle 4,-6\right\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero, so it gives a direction for the normal line. A line through the given point parallel to $\left\langle 4,-6\right\rangle$ satisfies

$$
\begin{aligned}
b(x-x_0)&=a(y-y_0) \\
\left(-6\right)\left(x - 1\right)&=\left(4\right)\left(y + 1\right) \\
- 6 x - 4 y + 2&=0 \\
3 x + 2 y - 1&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying the whole equation gives the normal line $3 x + 2 y - 1=0.$ Its direction is parallel to the gradient; using the gradient as the coefficient vector would give the tangent line instead.

Let $C$ be the straight segment from $A=(2,3)$ to $B=(2,2)$. Let $f(x,y)=e^{x+y}$. Which definite integral is equivalent to $\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$? Do not evaluate the integral.

The endpoint position vectors give

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r(t)&=\mathbf a+t(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\\
&=\langle 2,- t + 3\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=0$ and $t=1$ this gives $A=(2,3)$ and $B=(2,2)$, respectively.

Differentiate, compute the speed, and substitute both coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 0,-1\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(0)^2+(-1)^2}=1,\\
f(\mathbf r(t))&=e^{(2)+(- t + 3)}\\
&=e^{- t + 5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the scalar arc-length formula,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t,\\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(e^{- t + 5}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

The endpoints are $A=(3,1)$ and $B=(5,-1)$.

$$

\mathbf r(3)&=\langle 3,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $1\le u\le 3$ covers the segment from $B$ to $A$. Reversing traversal does not negate a scalar arc-length integral; its speed is positive.

Differentiate, compute the speed, and substitute both coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(u)&=\langle -1,1\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(u)\|&=\sqrt{(-1)^2+(1)^2}=\sqrt{2},\\
f(\mathbf r(u))&=e^{(- u + 6)+(u - 2)}\\
&=e^{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the scalar arc-length formula,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{1}^{3}f(\mathbf r(u))\,\|\mathbf r'(u)\|\,\mathrm{d}u,\\
&=\sqrt{2}\int_{1}^{3}\left(e^{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u.
\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r(t)&=\mathbf a+t(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\\
&=\langle t + 3,- t + 1\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=0$ and $t=1$ this gives $A=(3,1)$ and $B=(4,0)$, respectively.

Differentiate, compute the speed, and substitute both coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 1,-1\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(1)^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt{2},\\
f(\mathbf r(t))&=e^{(t + 3)+(- t + 1)}\\
&=e^{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t,\\
&=\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{1}\left(e^{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=2 x + 2 y$ along the line segment from $(3,-3)$ to $(3,0)$.

We will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{t_a}^{t_b} f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t,
$$

where $C$ is the line segment from $(3,-3)$ to $(3,0).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(3)\,i+(-3)\,j$ and $b=(3)\,i+(0)\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(3)\,i+(-3)\,j+t((0)\,i+(3)\,j) \\  & =(3)\,i+(3 \cdot t - 3)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=3$ and $y=3 \cdot t - 3$ along the segment.

Computing $r\prime(t)$ and $\|r\prime(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3)i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 \cdot t - 3)j \\  & =(0)\,i+(3)\,j \\ \|r\prime(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^2+(3)^2} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2 \cdot x + 2 \cdot y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(3)+2(3 \cdot t - 3) \\  & =6 \cdot t.\end{aligned}
$$

Write $I=\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_0^1 f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\int_0^1 (6 \cdot t)\cdot 3\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =3\int_0^1 (6 \cdot t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =3[3 \cdot t^{2}]_0^1 \\  & =3((3)+(0))-3(0) \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{t_a}^{t_b} f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t,
$$

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,3)$ to $(1,6).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(-1)\,i+(3)\,j$ and $b=(1)\,i+(6)\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-1)\,i+(3)\,j+t((2)\,i+(3)\,j) \\  & =(2 \cdot t - 1)\,i+(3 \cdot t + 3)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2 \cdot t - 1$ and $y=3 \cdot t + 3$ along the segment.

Computing $r\prime(t)$ and $\|r\prime(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 \cdot t - 1)i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(3 \cdot t + 3)j \\  & =(2)\,i+(3)\,j \\ \|r\prime(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(2)^2+(3)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\Phi=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds
=\sum_{k=1}^{4}\int_{C_k}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_k\,\mathrm ds.
$$

![Sides and outward normals](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179646/cdf46d05554fc51e0cbbc472b1dcc889b629195112d8faaea6789f38e2231823-solution.png)

The right, top, left and bottom sides have outward unit normals $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$, $-\mathbf i$ and $-\mathbf j$, respectively.

The uniform field is parallel to the top and bottom sides, so their normal components are zero. On the right and left sides the normal components are $-4$ and $4$. Each side has length $2$, so the signed contributions cancel:

$$
\begin{aligned}\Phi&=(-4)(2)+(4)(2)\\&=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The outward flux is

$$
\Phi=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds
=\sum_{k=1}^{4}\int_{C_k}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_k\,\mathrm ds.
$$

![Sides and outward normals](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179646/5b6ea7d030a2887c8aba898aa32d1f992f7bfdc223812c56199fce3525dbecdf-solution.png)

The right, top, left and bottom sides have outward unit normals $\mathbf i$, $\mathbf j$, $-\mathbf i$ and $-\mathbf j$, respectively.

The full field does not have equal side fluxes. Decompose it into radial and uniform parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf F&=\mathbf R+\mathbf U\\\mathbf R&=(- 2 x)\,\mathbf i+(- 2 y)\,\mathbf j\\\mathbf U&=(-1)\,\mathbf i+(-1)\,\mathbf j.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(\mathbf R+\mathbf U)\cdot\mathbf n=\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf n+\mathbf U\cdot\mathbf n$, the two fluxes add. The uniform part has opposite signed contributions on opposite sides of equal length:

$$
\Phi_{\mathbf U}=(-1)(2)+(-1)(2)-(-1)(2)-(-1)(2)=0.
$$

Now compute the radial part $\mathbf R$. On the right side $C_1$, use $\mathbf r(t)=1\,\mathbf i+t\,\mathbf j$ for $-1\le t\le 1$. Then $\mathbf n_1=\mathbf i$ and $\|\mathbf r\prime(t)\|=1$, so $\mathrm ds=\mathrm dt$. The radial normal component is $-2(1)=-2$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\Phi_1&=\int_{-1}^{1}(-2)\,\mathrm dt\\&=(-2)(1-(-1))\\&=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Quarter-turn symmetry preserves both the radial field and the outward normal component, so all four radial contributions are equal. Thus

$$
\Phi_{\mathbf R}=4(-4)=-16.
$$

Adding the uniform part gives $\Phi=-16+0=-16$. As a direct check, the full field gives:

| Side | Normal component | Flux |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Right | $-3$ | $-6$ |
| Top | $-3$ | $-6$ |
| Left | $-1$ | $-2$ |
| Bottom | $-1$ | $-2$ |

The four signed contributions sum to $-16$. Only the radial part has four equal contributions.

Write $P=- 3 x y^{2}$ and $Q=- 3 x^{2} y.$ A potential must satisfy $f_x=P$ and $f_y=Q$. Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives

$$
f(x,y)=- \frac{3 x^{2} y^{2}}{2}+g(y)
$$

Match its $y$ derivative to the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}- 3 x^{2} y+g'(y)&=- 3 x^{2} y \\ g'(y)&=0 \\ g(y)&=0+K\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $K=0$, since a constant cancels in the endpoint difference. Thus

$$
f(x,y)=- \frac{3 x^{2} y^{2}}{2}
$$

Differentiating verifies both components of the given field. For the stated orientation, the starting and ending points are

$$
\begin{aligned}A&=(4,1) \\ B&=(3,1)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(B)&=- \frac{3 \left(3\right)^{2} \left(1\right)^{2}}{2} \\ &=- \frac{27}{2} \\ f(A)&=- \frac{3 \left(4\right)^{2} \left(1\right)^{2}}{2} \\ &=-24\end{aligned}
$$

The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C F\cdot\mathrm{d}r & =\int_C\nabla f\cdot\mathrm{d}r \\  & =f(B)-f(A) \\  & =\left(- \frac{27}{2}\right)-\left(-24\right) \\  & =\frac{21}{2}.\end{aligned}

Given the function $f(x,y)=x^{2} y + 2 x y^{2} + 3 x y$, find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through $P=(2,1)$.

Hold the other coordinate constant when taking each partial derivative. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f_x(x,y)&=2 x y + 2 y^{2} + 3 y \\ f_y(x,y)&=x^{2} + 4 x y + 3 x \\ \nabla f(2,1)&=\langle 9,18\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero, so it is **normal** to the tangent line. Its dot product with the displacement along the line is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla f(2,1)\cdot\langle x - 2,y - 1\rangle&=0 \\ 9 x + 18 y - 36&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying or dividing the whole equation by a nonzero constant preserves the line. Thus the tangent equation is

$$
\langle 1,2\rangle\cdot\langle x - 2,y - 1\rangle=0
$$
Find the equation of the tangent line at $P=(1,0)$ to the curve $2 x e^{x y} - 2 y^{2}=- x^{2} - 3 y + 3$.

Move all terms to the left to define a level function:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y)&=x^{2} + 2 x e^{x y} - 2 y^{2} + 3 y - 3 \\ F(1,0)&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Apply the chain rule to the exponential and the product rule to its coordinate multiplier. 

$$
\begin{aligned}F_x(x,y)&=2 x + \left(2 x y + 2\right) e^{x y} \\ F_y(x,y)&=2 x^{2} e^{x y} - 4 y + 3 \\ \nabla F(1,0)&=\langle 4,5\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

The gradient is nonzero, so it is **normal** to the tangent line. Its dot product with the displacement along the line is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla F(1,0)\cdot\langle x - 1,y\rangle&=0 \\ 4 x + 5 y - 4&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying or dividing the whole equation by a nonzero constant preserves the line. Thus the tangent equation is

$$
4 x + 5 y - 4=0
$$

Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the following lines.

$$
\begin{aligned}2 x - y&=-3,\qquad 2 x - y=2, \\ x - 2 y&=-3,\qquad x - 2 y=1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 1: Choose coordinates.** Rewrite each boundary using its shared expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}2 x - y&=-3,\qquad 2 x - y=2, \\ x - 2 y&=-3,\qquad x - 2 y=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Choose $u=2 x - y$ and $v=x - 2 y$.

**Step 2: Map the boundaries.** The four boundaries become $u=-3$, $u=2$, $v=-3$, and $v=1$. Therefore

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v):-3\leq u\leq 2,\ -3\leq v\leq 1\}.
$$

![The transformed rectangle.](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186129262/rectangle-4c1e7a294f06da50.png)

**Step 3: Compute the forward Jacobian.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}2&-1 \\ 1&-2\end{vmatrix} \\ &=-3\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4: Take the reciprocal and its magnitude.** The inverse is

$$
\begin{aligned}x&=\frac{2 u}{3} - \frac{v}{3}, \\ y&=\frac{u}{3} - \frac{2 v}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant is nonzero, so this linear inverse is defined everywhere. Area uses the absolute value of the reciprocal determinant:

$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\left|\frac{1}{-3}\right|=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

**Step 5: Integrate over the rectangle.**

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\iint_{\Delta}\frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\int_{-3}^{1}\int_{-3}^{2}1\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dv \\ &=\frac{1}{3}\cdot\left(2-(-3)\right)\cdot\left(1-(-3)\right) \\ &=\frac{20}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}&=\begin{vmatrix}y&x \\ \frac{1}{y^{2}}&- \frac{2 x}{y^{3}}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=- \frac{3 x}{y^{2}} \\ &=- 3 v.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x&=u^{\frac{2}{3}} \sqrt[3]{v}, \\ y&=\frac{\sqrt[3]{u}}{\sqrt[3]{v}}.\end{aligned}
$$

These formulas give the unique positive inverse on the whole rectangle. Area uses the absolute value of the reciprocal determinant:

$$
\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\left|\frac{1}{- 3 v}\right|=\frac{1}{3 v}.

$$
